Package frc.robot.aiming

Class ToFAim

java.lang.Object
frc.robot.aiming.ToFAim
All Implemented Interfaces:
AimStrategy
public class ToFAim extends Object implements AimStrategy
Aim strategy that uses experimentally measured time-of-flight data to compute the ideal shot parameters for a moving robot.

What Is "Time of Flight"?

When a ball is fired, it travels through the air for some duration before reaching the hub. That duration â€” the time of flight (TOF) â€” depends on the straight-line distance from the shooter to the hub and on the launch angle and speed. Longer shots take longer. The TOF for this robot was measured by filming shots at known distances with a high-speed camera; those measurements are stored in ShooterConstants#scoringMeasurements as an AimMeasurement list and loaded into interpolating lookup tables in this class.

The Moving-Robot Problem

If the robot were stationary, aiming is simple: look up the distance to the hub, use the table to find the correct pitch and speed, and point the turret directly at the hub.

When the robot is moving, the ball inherits the robot's velocity in addition to the launch velocity. To compensate, the turret must aim at a different field-frame angle so the ball still arrives at the hub. Specifically, the required field-frame launch angle Î¸ is: 

   Î¸ = atan2(hub - (shooterPos + robotVelocity Ã— tof))
where shooterPos + robotVelocity Ã— tof is the position the shooter will be at when the ball arrives (call this afterShooting). The formula says: point the turret from the future robot position toward the hub â€” that direction, in field coordinates, is the angle the ball must leave the launcher at (adding the robot's field velocity gives the ball a path that arrives at the hub).

The Iterative Convergence Loop

There is a circular dependency: tof depends on distance, which depends on afterShooting, which depends on tof. We break this by iterating:
  1. Start with afterShooting = shooterPos (zero lead estimate).
  2. Compute distance from afterShooting to hub.
  3. Look up tof from the distance table.
  4. Compute a new afterShooting = shooterPos + velocity Ã— tof.
  5. If the new estimate changed less than EPSILON metres, we've converged â†’ stop.
  6. Otherwise repeat up to ITERATIONS times.
In practice, convergence happens in 3â€“4 iterations at FRC drive speeds. If after 15 iterations convergence has not been reached (robot is oscillating or sensor data is wildly noisy), the shot is declared Impossible.

Pitch and Speed

Once afterShooting has converged, the final distance d = |afterShooting - hub| is used to look up the correct hood pitch angle and shooter wheel speed from the tables. These values were measured at rest and are a good approximation even when moving because the distance correction is small (â‰ˆ1 m at 2 m/s for 0.5 s TOF).

Usage

An instance is created once in RobotStateMachine and called every control loop via LeadCompensator. Call it via update(Pose3d, Pose3d, Translation2d) each loop.

    • ToFAim

      public ToFAim(List<AimMeasurement> measurements, AimConstraints constraints)
      Builds the three interpolating lookup tables from the list of experimental measurements.
      Parameters:
      measurements - list of (distance, pitch, speed, time) data points; the more points and the wider the range, the more accurate extrapolation at the edges
      constraints - min/max hood angle and max output; shots outside these limits are marked Impossible so the robot doesn't attempt physically unreachable trajectories

      public AimParams update(edu.wpi.first.math.geometry.Pose3d aimTarget, edu.wpi.first.math.geometry.Pose3d shooterPose, edu.wpi.first.math.geometry.Translation2d shooterVelocity)
      Computes the aim parameters for the current robot state.

      This is the main entry point called each control loop (typically via LeadCompensator first, then this method with Translation2d.kZero velocity so lead compensation is not double-applied).

      Specified by:
      update in interface AimStrategy
      Parameters:
      aimTarget - target position in field coordinates â€” either the real hub or a lead-compensated virtual target from LeadCompensator
      shooterPose - current shooter pose in field coordinates
      shooterVelocity - robot field-relative velocity; pass Translation2d.kZero when lead compensation is handled externally by LeadCompensator
      Returns:
      computed shot parameters; status is AimParams.AimStatus.Impossible if the shot cannot converge or if the result violates constraints
